header: DEPARTMENT OF STATE, FOREIGN OPERATIONS, AND RELATED PROGRAMS APPROPRIATIONS ACT, 2016
summary:
**Division K — Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2016**

## Overview

This division funds the State Department, the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), and related foreign-affairs programs for fiscal year 2016. It pays for U.S. embassies and diplomats, humanitarian and development aid, global health, security assistance to partner countries, dues to international organizations, and U.S. contributions to development banks. The excerpt provided ends mid-Title VII (general provisions) and does not include a later title if one exists, so figures below are only what appears in the text.

## Total Spending

The text does not state one official grand total. Adding the main line-item appropriations in Titles I through V (and excluding loan guarantees’ “callable capital,” fee offsets, and accounts funded only by interest) comes to roughly **$39 billion**. That is an estimate from the line items, not an official score, and it may miss later titles or overseas-contingency funding not in this excerpt.

## Key Funding Areas

- **HIV/AIDS and related global health (State Department)**: $5.67 billion — prevention, treatment, and research on HIV/AIDS, available through September 30, 2020; the U.S. contribution to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria should be $1.35 billion.
- **Diplomatic and Consular Programs**: $5.62 billion — salaries, training, overseas posts, policy work, and security for the State Department and Foreign Service. Of that, up to $1.43 billion may be used for Worldwide Security Protection.
- **Foreign Military Financing**: $4.74 billion — grants so partner countries can buy U.S. defense articles and services. At least $3.1 billion is only for Israel, to be paid within 30 days of enactment; at least $815.3 million of Israel’s grant is for purchases in Israel.
- **Global health (USAID)**: $2.83 billion — maternal and child health, immunizations, nutrition, water and sanitation, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, other infectious diseases, and family planning.
- **Development Assistance**: $2.78 billion — longer-term development programs under the Foreign Assistance Act.
- **Economic Support Fund**: $1.90 billion — economic aid tied to U.S. foreign-policy goals.
- **Embassy security, construction, and maintenance**: $1.47 billion — $785.1 million for buildings and repairs (including the Harry S Truman Building) plus $688.8 million for worldwide security upgrades, acquisition, and construction.
- **Contributions to international organizations**: $1.34 billion — U.S. dues to multilateral organizations the United States belongs to, including the United Nations.
- **International Development Association**: $1.20 billion — U.S. payment to the World Bank’s fund for the poorest countries.
- **USAID operating expenses**: $1.14 billion — day-to-day costs of running the aid agency.

Other notable amounts: Migration and Refugee Assistance $931.9 million; Millennium Challenge Corporation $901 million; International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement $894.8 million; International Disaster Assistance $874.8 million; international broadcasting (Broadcasting Board of Governors) $734.1 million; peacekeeping assessments $666.6 million; educational and cultural exchanges $590.9 million (at least $236 million for Fulbright); nonproliferation, anti-terrorism, and demining $506.4 million; Europe, Eurasia, and Central Asia assistance $491.1 million; Peace Corps $410 million.

## Notable Provisions

- **Country floors and caps.** At least $1.275 billion for Jordan (including $204 million in budget support and $100 million for water); at least $658.2 million for Ukraine; up to $750 million for Central America under a U.S. engagement strategy; up to $150 million in economic aid and $1.3 billion in military aid for Egypt, with certifications and partial withholding; at least $141.9 million for Tunisia; at least $20 million for Libya; not more than $191.4 million for Haiti.
- **Democracy spending floor.** At least $2.31 billion across accounts for democracy programs (elections, human rights, independent media, rule of law, and related work). The National Endowment for Democracy gets $170 million.
- **Hard bans.** No direct aid under Titles III–VI to the governments of Cuba, North Korea, Iran, or Syria. Aid is also cut off to a government after a military coup until a democratically elected government takes office. No aid to the central government of Sudan or Russia, with narrow exceptions (for example, humanitarian aid).
- **Palestinian restrictions.** No Economic Support Fund money for the Palestinian Authority unless the President waives the ban for national security, for no more than six months at a time. No aid that honors people who committed terrorism. Aid is reduced by the amount the Palestinian Authority paid for acts of terrorism. No new U.S. office in Jerusalem to deal officially with the Palestinian Authority. No aid to the Palestinian Broadcasting Corporation. Funds for Hamas or a Hamas-controlled government are barred unless strict certifications are met.
- **Egypt conditions.** Fifteen percent of Egypt’s $1.3 billion military aid is withheld until the Secretary of State certifies steps on democracy, political prisoners, and accountability, with a national-security waiver. Economic aid equal to U.S. and NGO legal costs from certain democracy-related trials is withheld until specified convictions are dismissed.
- **Pakistan.** Economic, law-enforcement, and military aid requires a certification on counterterrorism cooperation (including against named groups), or a waiver. $33 million is withheld until the Secretary reports that Dr. Shakil Afridi has been released and cleared of charges tied to helping locate Osama bin Laden.
- **Afghanistan.** Aid may not go to people the Secretary finds corrupt or responsible for human rights abuses, to projects that cannot be sustained, or to new major infrastructure. The Secretary must certify transparency, anti-corruption, and women’s and girls’ rights steps, or waive that requirement.
- **Abortion and family planning.** Funds may not pay for abortion as a method of family planning, lobby for or against abortion, or support coercive abortion or involuntary sterilization. Peace Corps funds may not pay for abortions, with a cross-reference to an earlier law’s exception.
- **Israel-related items.** Loan-guarantee authority for Israel is extended to September 30, 2019. Congress states its opposition to the Arab League boycott of Israel. The Secretary should work to end that boycott.
- **Religious freedom and atrocities.** At least $10 million from the Democracy Fund’s human rights account for international religious freedom programs. The Secretary must evaluate whether attacks on Christians and other religious groups in the Middle East, and on Rohingya in Burma, constitute mass atrocities or genocide.
- **Embassy security after Benghazi.** Extra transfer authority between diplomatic operations and embassy construction to carry out Benghazi Accountability Review Board recommendations. A Foreign Affairs Security Training Center may receive up to $99.1 million only after a location analysis and congressional notice. At least $25 million for security at temporary facilities abroad.
- **Other limits.** No first-class travel in violation of federal rules. No funding to implement the Arms Trade Treaty until the Senate approves it. Cluster munitions may be transferred only if they meet a 1 percent unexploded-ordnance standard and use limits, or are being destroyed. No U.S. promotion of tobacco exports. Countries that tax U.S. aid can have later aid withheld at 200 percent of the tax if it is not reimbursed.

## Who Benefits

U.S. diplomats, embassy staff, and locally hired guards benefit from operating and security funds. People in poor countries benefit from health, education, food, water, and disaster aid—especially HIV/AIDS patients through the global AIDS program and the Global Fund. Refugees and host communities benefit from nearly $1 billion in migration and refugee funds plus disaster aid. Israel, Egypt, and Jordan are the largest named security-aid recipients. Ukraine and other Eastern Partnership countries get support tied to European agreements and pressure from Russia. Central American governments and communities are targeted to address migration of unaccompanied children. Democracy groups, the Peace Corps, broadcasters such as Voice of America, and development banks’ borrowing countries also receive funding.

## Plain English Summary

This is the 2016 budget for America’s diplomats and foreign aid. It keeps embassies open and safer, pays U.N. dues and peacekeeping bills, and sends billions overseas for HIV/AIDS, disaster relief, refugees, and long-term development. A large share of the security money is grants so allies—especially Israel, and also Egypt and Jordan—can buy American military equipment. Congress attached many strings: no checks to Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria, or post-coup governments; tight rules on Palestinian aid; and certifications before big packages for Egypt, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. If you picture the money, the biggest piles are global health, running the State Department, and arming partners—not a single new domestic program.

titles.header: DEPARTMENT OF STATE AND RELATED AGENCY
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

Title I funds the Department of State’s core diplomatic operations, embassy security and construction, educational and cultural exchanges, assessed dues to international organizations, and U.S. peacekeeping contributions. It also funds the Broadcasting Board of Governors, several related grant programs (including the National Endowment for Democracy, the U.S. Institute of Peace, The Asia Foundation, and the East-West Center), and five small commissions on heritage, religious freedom, and China/Europe oversight. Specified appropriations in the title total **$11,186,124,000**, plus fee authorities and three indefinite trust-fund interest appropriations.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| **Diplomatic and Consular Programs** | **$5,622,170,000** | State Department and Foreign Service operations not otherwise provided for |
| — Human resources | $2,181,622,000 | Training, HR management, and salaries (up to $358,833,000 for Worldwide Security Protection) |
| — Overseas programs | $1,561,840,000 | Regional bureaus and overseas activities |
| — Diplomatic policy and support | $791,121,000 | Functional bureaus, international-organization representation, administration, arms control/nonproliferation |
| — Security programs | $1,087,587,000 | Security activities (up to $1,069,635,000 for Worldwide Security Protection) |
| Capital Investment Fund | $66,400,000 | Department capital investments (available until expended) |
| Office of Inspector General | $72,700,000 | Inspector General operations ($10,905,000 available through Sept. 30, 2017) |
| Educational and Cultural Exchange Programs | $590,900,000 | Exchanges, including at least $236,000,000 for Fulbright and $102,000,000 for Citizen Exchanges ($4,000,000 of that for Congress-Bundestag Youth Exchange) |
| Representation Expenses | $8,030,000 | Official representation |
| Protection of Foreign Missions and Officials | $30,036,000 | Extraordinary protective services (available through Sept. 30, 2017) |
| Embassy Security, Construction, and Maintenance | $785,097,000 | Buildings owned or leased by State, Truman Building renovation, Diplomatic Security Construction Program |
| — Worldwide security upgrades (additional) | $688,799,000 | Worldwide security upgrades, acquisition, and construction |
| Emergencies in the Diplomatic and Consular Service | $7,900,000 | Unforeseen diplomatic/consular emergencies (up to $1,000,000 transferable to repatriation loans) |
| Repatriation Loans Program Account | $1,300,000 | Subsidy cost of direct loans (supports up to $2,444,528 in principal) |
| Payment to the American Institute in Taiwan | $30,000,000 | Taiwan Relations Act operations |
| Foreign Service Retirement and Disability Fund | $158,900,000 | Payment to the retirement and disability fund |
| Contributions to International Organizations | $1,344,458,000 | Assessed U.S. membership dues in multilateral organizations |
| Contributions for International Peacekeeping Activities | $666,574,000 | Assessed and other peacekeeping expenses (15% available through Sept. 30, 2017) |
| IBWC, U.S. and Mexico — Salaries and Expenses | $45,307,000 | U.S. Section salaries and expenses |
| IBWC — Construction | $28,400,000 | Plan preparation and construction of authorized projects |
| American Sections, International Commissions | $12,330,000 | International Joint Commission, U.S.-Canada Boundary Commission, and Border Environment Cooperation Commission |
| International Fisheries Commissions | $36,681,000 | U.S. share of international fisheries commission expenses |
| International Broadcasting Operations (BBG) | $734,087,000 | BBG international radio, Internet, and television, including Middle East broadcasting |
| Broadcasting Capital Improvements | $4,800,000 | Transmission facilities and equipment, including to Cuba, and physical security |
| The Asia Foundation | $17,000,000 | Grant under the Asia Foundation Act |
| United States Institute of Peace | $35,300,000 | USIP operations (not for construction; available through Sept. 30, 2017) |
| East-West Center | $16,700,000 | Grant to the Center for Cultural and Technical Interchange in Hawaii |
| National Endowment for Democracy | $170,000,000 | Grants via the State Department ($117,500,000 in the traditional manner, including core institutes; $52,500,000 for democracy programs) |
| Commission for the Preservation of America’s Heritage Abroad | $676,000 | Commission salaries and expenses |
| U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom | $3,500,000 | Commission salaries and expenses |
| Commission on Security and Cooperation in Europe | $2,579,000 | Helsinki Commission salaries and expenses |
| Congressional-Executive Commission on the PRC | $2,000,000 | Commission salaries and expenses |
| U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission | $3,500,000 | Commission salaries and expenses |

**No fixed dollar amount (interest and earnings only):** Center for Middle Eastern-Western Dialogue Trust Fund; Eisenhower Exchange Fellowship Program; Israeli Arab Scholarship Program.

**Additional fee/receipt authorities (not part of the $11.19 billion):** up to $1,840,900 plus $743,000 (International Center); up to $5,000,000 (exchange-program fees credited to Diplomatic and Consular Programs); up to $15,000 (Blair House); BBG receipts up to $5,000,000 (advertising/business ventures), $500,000 (cooperating organizations), and $1,000,000 (privatization).

Within Diplomatic and Consular Programs, up to $1,428,468,000 is for Worldwide Security Protection (available until expended), and up to $629,055,000 may remain available through September 30, 2017.

## Notable Sections

- **Foreign Affairs Security Training Center (FASTC):** Up to $99,113,000 under Diplomatic and Consular Programs may be obligated for FASTC only after the Secretary submits a cost-benefit analysis of at least three sites and gives Congress 15 days’ notice with a justification.
- **Religious-site restriction:** No Diplomatic and Consular Programs funds for preserving religious sites unless the Secretary finds the site historically, artistically, or culturally significant, the project neither advances nor inhibits free exercise of religion, and it is in the U.S. national interest.
- **J-1 Summer Work Travel:** Sponsors may not place student participants in seafood preparation or packaging in FY2016 unless they describe the program and verify compliance with exchange-visitor rules and the Act’s explanatory statement.
- **Peacekeeping conditions:** Funds cannot support a new or expanded UN mission without advance notice of cost, duration, objectives, U.S. interest, exit strategy, and funding source. Obligation also requires a mission-by-mission certification that the UN has policies against trafficking and sexual exploitation. Funds are unavailable if American manufacturers are not given equal opportunity to supply missions. U.S. forces may not serve under foreign command or operational control unless the President’s military advisors recommend it and the President submits that recommendation to Congress. Funding above the statutory assessment cap is allowed only up to the amount in Annex IV of UN General Assembly Resolution 64/220, and only with a national-interest determination.
- **UN dues limits:** No funds for the U.S. share of interest on international-organization loans incurred on or after October 1, 1984. Credits (including from the UN Tax Equalization Fund) may be used only for assessed UN contributions, with reporting and notification requirements. The Secretary must report within 180 days on steps to cut unnecessary UN administrative costs.
- **BBG conditions:** At least $15,000,000 of up to $31,135,000 set aside for satellite and Internet freedom must go to Internet freedom. The Board must notify Congress within 15 days if a broadcast entity provides an open platform for international terrorists or violates statutory broadcasting standards.
- **Other limits:** Diplomatic and Consular Programs may fund Conflict Stabilization Operations. A portion of Eurasia/Central Asia Fulbright awards must be designated Edmund S. Muskie Fellowships. USIP funds may not be used for construction. The Heritage Abroad Commission’s authority to procure temporary services ends October 1, 2016.

## Plain English

This title pays for U.S. embassies, diplomats, passport and consular services, embassy security, UN membership and peacekeeping dues, U.S. international broadcasting, and a set of exchange, democracy, and oversight programs.

titles.header: UNITED STATES AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

Title II appropriates administrative funds to the President for the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) under section 667 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. It covers agency operating expenses, capital investments (overseas construction and information technology), and the USAID Office of Inspector General—not foreign assistance program accounts.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Operating Expenses | $1,143,614,000 | Necessary expenses to carry out section 667 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (USAID operations). Up to $171,542,000 may remain available until September 30, 2017. |
| — of which, representation and entertainment | Not to exceed $250,000 | Representation and entertainment expenses for USAID in the current fiscal year. |
| — of which, entertainment | Not to exceed $5,000 | Entertainment expenses (within the $250,000 cap). |
| — of which, official residence expenses | Not to exceed $100,500 | Official residence expenses for USAID. |
| Capital Investment Fund | $168,300,000 | Overseas construction and related costs, and procurement and enhancement of information technology and related capital investments; available until expended, in addition to funds otherwise available for such purposes. |
| Office of Inspector General | $66,000,000 | Necessary expenses for the USAID Office of Inspector General. Up to $9,900,000 may remain available until September 30, 2017. |
| **Total** | **$1,377,914,000** | |

## Notable Sections

- **Office space restriction:** None of the Operating Expenses or Capital Investment Fund may finance construction (including architect and engineering services), purchase, or long-term lease of offices for USAID unless the Administrator identifies the proposed use in a report to the Committees on Appropriations at least 15 days before obligation.
- **Forward funding of contracts:** Contracts or agreements under Operating Expenses may commit funds through the following fiscal year.
- **Transfer authority:** The Secretary of State may use sections 610 and 109 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 to transfer funds appropriated to carry out chapter 1 of part I of that Act into Operating Expenses.
- **Notification:** Capital Investment Fund amounts are subject to the regular notification procedures of the Committees on Appropriations.
- No new programs are created. The provisions are administrative limits, multi-year availability, and congressional notification requirements.

## Plain English

This title pays for USAID’s own staff, offices, technology, overseas construction, and inspector general—the cost of running the foreign-aid agency—not the aid programs themselves.

## Title Summary

Title III appropriates bilateral economic and humanitarian assistance, chiefly under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, for global health, development, disaster relief, democracy, and refugee programs. Funds go primarily to the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) and the Department of State, with separate accounts for the Peace Corps, Millennium Challenge Corporation, Inter-American Foundation, U.S. African Development Foundation, and the Treasury Department’s technical-assistance program.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Global Health Programs (USAID) | $2,833,450,000 | Child survival, maternal health, immunization, nutrition, water and sanitation, HIV/AIDS, TB, polio, malaria, other infectious diseases, disaster-preparedness training, and family planning/reproductive health; available through Sept. 30, 2017. May include a contribution to the GAVI Alliance. |
| Global Health Programs (State — HIV/AIDS) | $5,670,000,000 | Prevention, treatment, control of, and research on HIV/AIDS, apportioned to the Department of State; available through Sept. 30, 2020. Of this, the U.S. contribution to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria should be $1,350,000,000. Up to 5% of FY2016 Global Fund funds may go to USAID for related technical assistance. Up to $17,000,000 may cover administrative expenses of the Office of the U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator. |
| Development Assistance | $2,780,971,000 | Development programs under specified sections of the Foreign Assistance Act; available through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| International Disaster Assistance | $874,763,000 | International disaster relief, rehabilitation, and reconstruction; available until expended. |
| Transition Initiatives | $30,000,000 | USAID Office of Transition Initiatives support for countries in crisis (democratic institutions, basic infrastructure, peaceful conflict resolution); available until expended. If the Secretary of State finds it in the national interest, up to $15,000,000 more may be used from other part I foreign-assistance funds, after consultation with Appropriations Committees. |
| Complex Crises Fund | $10,000,000 | Programs to prevent or respond to emerging or unforeseen foreign challenges and complex crises; available until expended. No lethal assistance and no response to natural disasters. Administrative expenses may not exceed 5%. |
| Development Credit Authority (transfer authority) | Up to $40,000,000 (by transfer) | Subsidy cost of USAID direct loans and loan guarantees for micro- and small-enterprise, urban, and related programs. May support up to $1,500,000,000 in total loan principal; no single country may exceed $300,000,000 in principal. |
| Development Credit Authority (administrative expenses) | $8,120,000 | Administrative costs of USAID credit programs; available through Sept. 30, 2018. May be transferred to and merged with Operating Expenses. |
| Economic Support Fund | $1,896,315,000 | Economic and political support under chapter 4 of part II of the Foreign Assistance Act; available through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| Democracy Fund | $150,500,000 | Global democracy promotion; available through Sept. 30, 2017. Of this, $88,500,000 for State’s Human Rights and Democracy Fund (Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor) and $62,000,000 for USAID’s Bureau for Democracy, Conflict, and Humanitarian Assistance. |
| Assistance for Europe, Eurasia and Central Asia | $491,119,000 | Assistance for countries covered by the FREEDOM Support Act and the SEED Act; available through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| Migration and Refugee Assistance | $931,886,000 | Refugee and migration needs under the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962; available until expended. Not less than $35,000,000 for small-scale emergency humanitarian requirements; $10,000,000 for refugees resettling in Israel. |
| U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund | $50,000,000 | Emergency refugee and migration assistance under section 2(c) of the 1962 Act; available until expended. |
| Peace Corps | $410,000,000 | Peace Corps operations; available through Sept. 30, 2017. Includes $5,150,000 for the Office of Inspector General. Up to $5,000,000 may be transferred to the Foreign Currency Fluctuations Account (not from overseas operations funds). Representation expenses capped at $104,000, of which entertainment may not exceed $4,000. |
| Millennium Challenge Corporation | $901,000,000 | Compacts and related programs under the Millennium Challenge Act of 2003; available until expended. Up to $105,000,000 for administrative expenses; up to 5% may carry out section 616 of the Act for FY2016. Representation and entertainment capped at $100,000, of which entertainment may not exceed $5,000. |
| Inter-American Foundation | $22,500,000 | Foundation programs in Latin America and the Caribbean; available through Sept. 30, 2017. Representation expenses capped at $2,000. |
| U.S. African Development Foundation | $30,000,000 | Foundation programs in Africa; available through Sept. 30, 2017. Representation expenses capped at $2,000. |
| International Affairs Technical Assistance (Treasury) | $23,500,000 | Technical assistance under section 129 of the Foreign Assistance Act; available through Sept. 30, 2018, notwithstanding any other provision of law. |

Direct appropriations in this title total **$17,114,124,000**. The $40 million Development Credit Authority figure is transfer authority, not new budget authority. The Global Fund, coordinator, Israel-refugee, and small-scale emergency amounts are set-asides within larger accounts, not additions.

## Notable Sections

- **Family planning and abortion restrictions (Global Health Programs).** Funds may not go to any organization or program the President determines supports or participates in coercive abortion or involuntary sterilization; that determination must be made within 6 months and accompanied by the evidence and criteria used. Funds may not pay for abortion as a method of family planning, motivate or coerce abortion, or lobby for or against abortion. Existing prohibitions in section 104 of the Foreign Assistance Act are unchanged. Voluntary family-planning projects must offer a broad range of methods and meet detailed rules against quotas, incentives, denial of benefits for refusing services, and inadequate risk information; experimental methods are limited to scientific studies. USAID must report certain violations to the Appropriations Committees. Applicants offering only natural family planning may not be discriminated against for religious or conscientious reasons. “Motivate” does not bar information or counseling about all pregnancy options consistent with local law. Condom information funded by the Act must be medically accurate and include public-health benefits and failure rates.
- **Global Fund and PEPFAR adjustments.** The State HIV/AIDS account may fund the Global Fund notwithstanding other law except the U.S. Leadership Against HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria Act. For FY2015 and FY2016 funds, specified provisions of that Act are applied by substituting “2004” for “2009.”
- **Complex Crises Fund limits.** Funds may be used notwithstanding most other law, but not sections 7007, 7008, and 7018 of this Act or section 620M of the Foreign Assistance Act, and not for lethal assistance or natural disasters. Obligations require notification at least 5 days in advance.
- **Peace Corps abortion restriction.** None of the Peace Corps funds may be used to pay for abortions, except as provided by section 614 of division E of Public Law 113–76. Opening, closing, or significantly reducing an office or country program generally requires prior consultation and notification, waivable for a substantial security risk.
- **Millennium Challenge Corporation eligibility changes.** The title modifies candidate-country income rules relative to the World Bank’s lower-middle-income threshold and the 75 lowest-income countries, lets a country keep its prior income classification for the year of reclassification and the next two fiscal years, bars threshold programs after a country has completed a compact and in countries that are not current candidates, and directs a Comptroller General review—paid on a reimbursable basis from these funds—of authorities to obligate prior-year unobligated funds for compacts in countries not currently eligible.
- **Country-specific and institutional earmarks.** Migration and Refugee Assistance includes $10 million for refugees resettling in Israel. The Democracy Fund is split between State and USAID. The African Development Foundation may, in exceptional circumstances, waive its $250,000 project cap by up to 10% solely for foreign-currency fluctuation and must report each waiver.

## Plain English

This title funds U.S. foreign aid for health, development, disasters, democracy, and refugees—about $17.1 billion—through USAID, the State Department, the Peace Corps, and smaller independent agencies, with detailed limits on how family-planning money can be used.

## Title Summary

Title IV funds Department of State and presidential security-assistance programs for fiscal year 2016: counternarcotics and foreign law enforcement, nonproliferation and demining, peacekeeping, military training, and foreign military financing grants. The largest account is Foreign Military Financing, with a statutory floor for Israel and availability for Jordan and Egypt subject to section 7041 of the Act. Appropriations under the title total **$6,378,200,000**.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement | $894,821,000 | Carry out FAA §481 (narcotics control and law enforcement); available until Sept. 30, 2017 |
| — transfer to Assistance for Europe, Eurasia and Central Asia | not less than $54,975,000 | Merged with that account; same purposes as this heading |
| Nonproliferation, Anti-terrorism, Demining and Related Programs | $506,381,000 | Anti-terrorism assistance, nonproliferation, demining, UXO clearance, small-arms destruction, CTBT Preparatory Commission, and a voluntary IAEA contribution; available until Sept. 30, 2017 |
| Peacekeeping Operations | $131,361,000 | FAA §551 peacekeeping assistance, including capacity of foreign civilian security forces |
| — Multinational Force and Observers (Sinai) | not less than $35,000,000 | U.S. contribution to the Sinai MFO |
| International Military Education and Training | $108,115,000 | FAA §541 military education and training; up to $4,000,000 may remain available until Sept. 30, 2017 |
| — entertainment (IMET) | not to exceed $55,000 | Entertainment expenses |
| Foreign Military Financing Program | $4,737,522,000 | Nonrepayable grants under Arms Export Control Act §23 for defense articles and services |
| — Israel | not less than $3,100,000,000 | Grants only for Israel; disbursed within 30 days of enactment |
| — procurement in Israel | not less than $815,300,000 | Of the Israel grants, for procurement in Israel of defense articles and services, including R&D, if Israel requests it |
| — FMF administration | not more than $75,000,000 | General costs of administering military assistance and sales (passenger vehicles for replacement only, outside the U.S.) |
| — entertainment / representation (FMF admin) | not to exceed $4,000 / $130,000 | Within the administration cap |
| **Total appropriated** | **$6,378,200,000** | Sum of the five appropriation headings |

A separate cap—not a new appropriation—limits to **$904,000,000** the FY2016 obligation of funds realized under Arms Export Control Act §21(e)(1)(A) for Department of Defense expenses under §43(b).

## Notable Sections

- **Israel FMF terms:** At least $3.1 billion in grants only, paid within 30 days; at least $815.3 million available for in-Israel procurement, including research and development. Jordan and Egypt assistance is conditioned on section 7041.
- **IAEA and Iran reporting:** NADR funds may go to the IAEA unless the Secretary of State determines Israel is denied its right to participate. The Secretary must inform congressional committees of any separate arrangements on the IAEA–Iran “Road-map” on outstanding nuclear issues, in classified form if necessary.
- **U.S.-origin ordnance:** For unexploded-ordnance clearance, the Secretary should prioritize areas where the ordnance was caused by the United States.
- **INCLE flexibilities:** $54,975,000 must move to the Europe/Eurasia/Central Asia account; FAA §482(b) does not apply (with notification); State may receive excess U.S. property for transfer abroad; funds support training of foreign law enforcement, corrections, and judicial authorities via regional partners.
- **Peacekeeping waiver:** Funds may assist foreign civilian security forces, including gendarmes, notwithstanding FAA §660. No peacekeeping funds may be obligated except through Appropriations Committee notification.
- **Program continuity limits:** FMF may not support or continue programs first funded under NDAA FY2006 §1206 or 10 U.S.C. §2282 unless State, with Defense, justifies them to the Appropriations Committees. Only countries justified for Foreign Military Sales financing in the FY1989 congressional presentation may use these funds to buy items not sold by the U.S. Government under the Arms Export Control Act.
- **IMET civilians:** Training may cover civilians who are not government members if participation would improve civil-military relations, civilian control of the military, or respect for human rights.

## Plain English

This title spends about $6.4 billion to train and equip foreign security forces, fight narcotics and terrorism abroad, clear mines and unexploded weapons, and support peacekeeping—with more than $3 billion of the military-financing grants reserved for Israel.

## Title Summary

Title V funds U.S. voluntary contributions to international organizations and U.S. payments to multilateral development banks and related trust funds, administered through the President and the Secretary of the Treasury. It covers the International Organizations and Programs account plus capital and fund contributions to the World Bank Group, regional development banks, and several climate and agriculture facilities. Most bank and fund payments remain available until expended.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|

## Notable Sections

- **IPCC/UNFCCC set-aside:** Up to $10 million of the international organizations account may be used for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change. Separate climate-related payments go to the GEF ($168.3 million), Clean Technology Fund ($170.7 million), and Strategic Climate Fund ($49.9 million).
- **U.N. Democracy Fund waiver:** Section 307(a) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 does not apply to contributions to the United Nations Democracy Fund, so that statutory restriction is waived for those contributions.
- **Callable capital:** Governors (or, for NADB, the Secretary of the Treasury) may subscribe, without fiscal-year limitation, to large callable-capital shares. These are contingent commitments, not appropriated outlays.
- No new programs are created; the title funds existing organizations, banks, and funds.

## Plain English

This title sends about $2.62 billion in U.S. taxpayer funds to international organizations and development banks that finance global development, environment, climate, and agriculture programs, and it also authorizes several billion dollars in contingent capital commitments that are not immediate cash spending.

## Title Summary

Title VI funds U.S. export credit, overseas investment insurance, and trade-development activities. It covers the Export-Import Bank of the United States (Inspector General, program authority, and administrative expenses), the Overseas Private Investment Corporation (administrative expenses and loan-subsidy costs), and the Trade and Development Agency.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Export-Import Bank — Inspector General | $6,000,000 | Office of Inspector General expenses under the Inspector General Act; available until September 30, 2017 |
| Export-Import Bank — administrative expenses | Not to exceed $106,250,000 | Direct and guaranteed loan and insurance program administration, including hire of passenger vehicles and limited expert services; includes up to $30,000 for Board reception and representation |
| Export-Import Bank — offsetting receipts | General Fund net estimated at $0 | Receipts under the Export-Import Bank Act and Federal Credit Reform Act credited as offsetting collections, reducing the General Fund appropriation dollar-for-dollar to an estimated $0 |
| Export-Import Bank — excess collections | Up to $10,000,000 | FY2016 collections above obligations, available September 1, 2016, through September 30, 2019 |
| OPIC — administrative expenses (noncredit account) | Not to exceed $62,787,000 | Credit and insurance program administration; official reception and representation capped at $35,000; project-specific transaction and claims costs excluded from this cap |
| OPIC — program account (loan subsidy) | $20,000,000 | Cost of direct and guaranteed loans under section 234 of the Foreign Assistance Act, transferred from the OPIC Noncredit Account; available for obligations in FY2016–FY2018, with disbursement windows through 2024, 2025, and 2026 respectively |
| Trade and Development Agency | $60,000,000 | Activities under section 661 of the Foreign Assistance Act; available until September 30, 2017. Up to $2,500,000 may support procurement advice to foreign governments on U.S.-funded local procurements (USAID, MCC, State). Representation and entertainment capped at $5,000 |

The Export-Import Bank program heading authorizes expenditures and commitments within available funds and borrowing authority; it does not state a separate dollar appropriation.

## Notable Sections

- **Nuclear-export restriction (Ex-Im):** No funds available in the fiscal year may support expenditures, contracts, or commitments for export of nuclear equipment, fuel, or technology to any country—other than an NPT nuclear-weapon state eligible for economic or military assistance under the Act—that detonates a nuclear explosive after enactment.
- **Fee and participant-payment authority (Ex-Im):** The Bank may accept and use payments or services from transaction participants for legal, financial, or technical work, and may credit certain collection, collateral, appraisal, and transaction-evaluation fees to the administrative account until expended.
- **Iraq authority (OPIC):** Notwithstanding other law, OPIC may undertake programs authorized by title IV of chapter 2 of part I of the Foreign Assistance Act in Iraq, subject to the regular notification procedures of the Appropriations Committees.
- **Multi-year credit window (OPIC):** The $20,000,000 subsidy may support obligations made in FY2016, FY2017, or FY2018, with disbursement availability extending as far as 2026 depending on the year of obligation.

## Plain English

This title pays for the federal agencies that help U.S. companies finance exports and invest abroad, while barring Ex-Im support for certain nuclear exports to countries that conduct a new nuclear detonation.

**Title VII — General Provisions** (Division K, FY2016 State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs) does not create a new agency budget. It sets rules, conditions, transfer authorities, and country-specific floors and ceilings that govern how funds appropriated elsewhere in the Act may be used.

## Title Summary

This title applies to the Department of State, the Broadcasting Board of Governors (now the U.S. Agency for Global Media), USAID, and foreign-assistance accounts in Titles I–VI. It covers embassy security and construction, transfers and reprogramming, congressional notification, and restrictions on aid to specified countries and entities. It also sets minimums and caps for democracy, religious freedom, and bilateral programs in the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and the Western Hemisphere.

These figures are directions on money already appropriated in other titles, not new standalone appropriations.

## Spending Breakdown

| Jordan (Titles III and IV) | Not less than $1,275,000,000, including not less than $204,000,000 budget support and $100,000,000 water-sector support | Bilateral aid, including response to the Syria crisis |

Notification and reprogramming thresholds in the title (not program funding) include $1,000,000 (or 10%, whichever is less) for many reprogrammings; $7,000,000 for certain excess-defense-article sales; $10,000,000 for most direct government-to-government aid; and $3,000,000 / $2,000,000 reporting triggers for certain local-entity awards.

## Notable Sections

- **Country bans and coup rule (Secs. 7007–7008, 7012).** No direct aid or Export-Import Bank financing for the governments of Cuba, North Korea, Iran, or Syria. Aid to a government installed by a military coup is cut off until a democratically elected government takes office, with a narrow exception for election and participation programs. Countries more than one year in default on U.S. loans are barred unless the President finds aid is in the national interest.
- **Abortion and sterilization (Sec. 7018).** No funds under part I of the Foreign Assistance Act may pay for abortions as family planning, motivate or coerce abortion, or pay for involuntary sterilization or related biomedical research.
- **Palestinian restrictions (Secs. 7036–7040, 7041(j)).** No support for a Palestinian state without certifications on peaceful coexistence and counterterrorism (presidential waiver). No new U.S. office in Jerusalem to conduct business with the Palestinian Authority. Ban on aid to the Palestinian Broadcasting Corporation. Economic Support Fund for the West Bank and Gaza requires vetting against terrorist activity. Direct chapter-4 aid to the Palestinian Authority is prohibited unless waived for no more than 6 months at a time. No salaries for PA personnel in Gaza and no aid to Hamas or a Hamas-influenced government without certification. ESF is reduced by the amount the Secretary finds the PA paid for acts of terrorism. Aid is also restricted if the Palestinians obtain UN-member standing outside a negotiated agreement or support an ICC investigation of Israeli nationals.
- **Egypt, Pakistan, and other certifications (Secs. 7041, 7044).** Egypt FMF is partly withheld pending steps on democracy, expression, political prisoners, and security-force accountability. ESF is withheld in an amount tied to costs of specified democracy-related trials until convictions are dismissed. Pakistan aid under three headings requires a counterterrorism certification (waiver allowed). FMF for Pakistan is limited to counterterrorism and counterinsurgency.
- **Central America migration package (Sec. 7045(a)).** Up to $750 million, with 25% and then an additional 50% of aid to the central governments of El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras withheld until certifications on migration, corruption, justice, policing, and revenue, among other steps.
- **Embassy security (Sec. 7004).** Agencies that have not paid their capital-security cost share cannot get office space in new diplomatic facilities (Marines excepted). Funds other than London property-sale proceeds may not be used for the New London Embassy. Extra reporting is required on Mexico City and Beirut projects. Transfer authority is provided to implement Benghazi Accountability Review Board recommendations.
- **Anti-kleptocracy visas and transparency (Sec. 7031).** Officials and immediate family members credibly linked to significant corruption or gross human-rights violations are ineligible for U.S. entry, with law-enforcement, UN Headquarters, and national-interest exceptions. Direct government-to-government aid requires financial-management, procurement, budget-disclosure, and civil-society conditions. No funds may pay another country’s debt service to an international financial institution.
- **Religious freedom (Sec. 7033).** Funding floors and program direction for the religious-freedom office and envoy; a required evaluation of whether persecution of Christians and other religious people in the Middle East, and of Rohingya in Burma, constitutes mass atrocities or genocide.

titles.header: OVERSEAS CONTINGENCY OPERATIONS/GLOBAL WAR ON TERRORISM
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

Title VIII provides **$14,895,000,000** in additional fiscal year 2016 funding, designated as Overseas Contingency Operations/Global War on Terrorism (OCO/GWOT) under the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act. It covers the Department of State, the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), the Broadcasting Board of Governors, and related foreign assistance accounts—embassy operations and security, international organizations and peacekeeping, disaster and refugee aid, economic support, and security assistance. These amounts are **in addition to** base appropriations in the Act (Sec. 8001) and generally carry the same authorities and conditions as those accounts (Sec. 8002).

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Diplomatic and Consular Programs | $2,561,808,000 | State operations through Sept. 30, 2017; **$1,966,632,000** for Worldwide Security Protection (until expended). Up to **$10,000,000** may be transferred for Afghanistan operations; up to **$15,000,000** for conflict stabilization. |
| Office of Inspector General | $66,600,000 | Oversight through Sept. 30, 2017; **$56,900,000** for the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR). |
| Embassy Security, Construction, and Maintenance | $747,851,000 | Embassy security and construction until expended; **$735,201,000** for Worldwide Security Upgrades, acquisition, and construction. |
| Contributions to International Organizations | $101,728,000 | Additional U.S. assessments to international organizations. |
| Contributions for International Peacekeeping Activities | $1,794,088,000 | U.N. and other assessed peacekeeping, available through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| International Broadcasting Operations | $10,700,000 | Broadcasting Board of Governors operations through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| USAID Operating Expenses | $139,262,000 | USAID operating costs through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| International Disaster Assistance | $1,919,421,000 | Disaster relief, available until expended. Up to **$600,000,000** may be transferred to Migration and Refugee Assistance. |
| Transition Initiatives | $37,000,000 | Short-term transition assistance, available until expended. |
| Complex Crises Fund | $20,000,000 | Flexible response to emerging crises, available until expended. |
| Economic Support Fund | $2,422,673,000 | Economic and political assistance through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| Assistance for Europe, Eurasia and Central Asia | $438,569,000 | Assistance for that region through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| Migration and Refugee Assistance | $2,127,114,000 | Refugee crises in Africa, the Near East, South and Central Asia, and Europe and Eurasia; available until expended. **May not** pay U.S. refugee resettlement costs. |
| International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement | $371,650,000 | Counternarcotics and law enforcement assistance through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| Nonproliferation, Anti-terrorism, Demining and Related Programs | $379,091,000 | Nonproliferation, counterterrorism, and demining through Sept. 30, 2017. |
| Peacekeeping Operations | $469,269,000 | Voluntary peacekeeping support through Sept. 30, 2017; may pay assessed peacekeeping expenses in Somalia within the Title I cap, with committee notification. |
| Foreign Military Financing Program | $1,288,176,000 | Grants for foreign military purchases through Sept. 30, 2017. Up to **$15,000,000** (Europe and Eurasia) may move to the Global Security Contingency Fund for that region only. |
| **Total** | **$14,895,000,000** | All amounts OCO/GWOT-designated. |

## Notable Sections

- **OCO designation (every account):** Congress designates the entire title under section 251(b)(2)(A)(ii), so these funds sit outside ordinary discretionary caps. Sec. 8001 states they are additive to FY2016 base funding.
- **Afghanistan flexibility:** The Secretary of State may transfer up to $10,000,000 from Diplomatic and Consular Programs to any other department or agency for Afghanistan operations and Foreign Assistance Act activities, treated as a reprogramming under section 7015.
- **SIGAR personnel (Inspector General):** Employees with 12 months of continuous service after enactment, or employed when SIGAR ends, gain competitive status for federal competitive-service jobs. Printing and reproduction costs may not exceed FY2015 levels.
- **No U.S. resettlement from this MRA money:** The $2,127,114,000 for Migration and Refugee Assistance is barred from refugee resettlement costs inside the United States.
- **Somalia peacekeeping:** Peacekeeping Operations funds may cover assessed expenses in Somalia, capped at the level set in the Title I peacekeeping proviso, with Appropriations Committee notification.
- **Sec. 8003 transfer authority:** Funds may be moved among economic accounts (Transition Initiatives, Complex Crises Fund, Economic Support Fund, Assistance for Europe, Eurasia and Central Asia) and among security accounts (narcotics/law enforcement, nonproliferation, peacekeeping operations, foreign military financing), but only to address contingencies, and only after consultation and notification of the Appropriations Committees. Up to $600,000,000 may shift from International Disaster Assistance to Migration and Refugee Assistance. Authority is in addition to section 610 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961.

## Plain English

This title adds about $14.9 billion—outside normal budget limits—for embassy security, overseas disaster and refugee aid, peacekeeping, and military and economic assistance tied to conflicts abroad, and it does not pay to resettle refugees in the United States.

## Title Summary

Title IX implements the 2010 IMF quota reform. It appropriates an increase in the U.S. quota in the International Monetary Fund equal to the dollar equivalent of 40,871,800,000 Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and permanently rescinds the same SDR amount from the U.S. credit line under the IMF’s New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB) once the quota increase takes effect. It also amends the Bretton Woods Agreements Act and adds congressional reporting and voting restrictions on IMF exceptional-access lending. No fixed U.S. dollar figure is stated in the title.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| United States Quota, IMF (direct loan program account) | Dollar equivalent of SDR 40,871,800,000 (available until expended) | Increase the U.S. quota in the IMF; scored on a present-value basis using a Treasury rate adjusted for market risk; available only if the President designates it an emergency requirement |
| Loans to the IMF (direct loan program account) — rescission | Dollar equivalent of SDR 40,871,800,000 permanently rescinded | Roll back the U.S. NAB credit arrangement from the Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2009 (P.L. 111–32), no earlier than when the quota increase is effective; also requires a presidential emergency designation |

The two amounts are equal and designed to offset. Budgetary cost is the present-value subsidy (with market risk), not the full SDR face amount.

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 9001 — NAB limits and expiration.** U.S. authority to lend under the NAB expires December 16, 2022. Before activation, Treasury must certify that the IMF’s one-year forward commitment capacity (excluding borrowed resources) is expected to fall below SDR 100,000,000,000 and that activation is in the U.S. strategic economic interest, and must consult Congress.
- **Sec. 9002 — Quota increase authority.** Authorizes the U.S. Governor to accept the amendments in IMF Board of Governors resolution 66–2 and to consent to the SDR 40,871,800,000 quota increase, only to the extent provided in appropriations acts.
- **Sec. 9003 — CBO scoring review.** Requires a CBO report within 180 days on how market risk is built into IMF cost estimates, and directs the Appropriations and Budget Committees to review that methodology.
- **Sec. 9004 — Exceptional-access consultations.** Bars the U.S. Executive Director from voting for an exceptional-access loan unless Treasury has given Congress a program report and debt-sustainability analysis at least 7 days in advance (or within 2 business days afterward in a certified emergency). Submissions may be classified.
- **Sec. 9005 — Systemic-risk exemption.** Directs Treasury to press the IMF to repeal the systemic-risk exemption to the debt-sustainability test for exceptional access. The quota increase may not be disbursed until Treasury reports that the United States has taken all necessary steps to secure that repeal.
- **Secs. 9006–9007 — Reporting.** Annual Treasury reports on IMF lending, surveillance, and technical-assistance policy through 2025, plus a 180-day report on risks, transparency, exceptional-access loans, and lessons from “Troika” lending in the European debt crisis.

## Plain English

The United States raises its ownership share in the IMF by the same amount it cuts a backup lending commitment, and Congress gets more say before the U.S. supports large IMF rescue loans.
